stem: On a common electric cell used in a torch, which part is its positive terminal?
options: The flat metal disc at the other end
The raised metal cap at one end
The plastic or paper cover around it
The middle part of its metal body
explanation: Correct option: (B). The metal cap of a cell is its positive terminal, marked +. The flat metal disc is the negative terminal, not the positive one. The outer cover and the middle of the body are not terminals at all.

stem: What is a combination of two or more electric cells joined together called?
options: A battery
A filament
A switch
A conductor
explanation: Correct option: (A). Two or more cells joined with the positive terminal of one to the negative terminal of the next form a battery. A filament is the thin glowing wire of a lamp, a switch completes or breaks a circuit, and a conductor is a material that lets current pass.

stem: Riya puts two working cells into her torch, but the working lamp does not glow when she switches it on. What is the most likely reason?
options: Each cap touches the disc of the next cell
The two cells are placed in a single line
The torch switch was slid to the ON position
One cell is reversed, so like ends touch
explanation: Correct option: (D). The lamp glows only when the positive terminal of one cell touches the negative terminal of the next. If one cell is reversed, two like terminals touch and the cells do not work together. A cap touching the next disc is the correct order, placing cells in one line is how a torch holds them, and switching ON is needed for the lamp to glow, so none of these stops it.

stem: A wall clock and a TV remote work without being plugged into a wall socket. Which statement best explains this?
options: They store wall-socket electricity in their wires
They make electricity from light falling on them
They run on cells, a portable source of energy
They need no electrical energy as they are small

stem: In a two-cell torch, the cap of cell 1 touches the lamp, the cap of cell 2 touches the disc of cell 1, and the disc of cell 2 touches the spring. Which change will stop the working lamp from glowing?
options: Turning only cell 2 around, so its disc meets cell 1's disc
Replacing both cells with new ones placed the same way
Swapping the two cells, keeping each facing the same way
Replacing the lamp with another working torch lamp
explanation: Correct option: (A). If only cell 2 is turned around, its negative disc meets the negative disc of cell 1, so like terminals touch and the cells no longer form a battery. New cells placed the same way, or swapping the cells without turning them, still keep each cap against the next disc. A working replacement lamp does not change the cell order, so the lamp still glows in those cases.

The metal case at the base
The thin filament wire
The glass of the bulb

It is attached to the shorter wire
It is the wire joined to the filament

stem: A torch lamp does not glow even with fresh cells, and the thin wire inside its glass bulb is seen to be broken. Which statement best explains this?
options: The glass blocks the light once the filament breaks
The cells stop making energy when the lamp is broken
Current now flows only through the thick support wires
The broken filament leaves no complete path for current
explanation: Correct option: (D). The lamp has 'fused': a broken filament stops the flow of current, so the circuit is not complete and the lamp cannot glow. stem: Which statement correctly compares an LED with an incandescent lamp?
options: An LED has one terminal, but an incandescent lamp has two
An LED has no filament, but an incandescent lamp has one
An LED has a filament, but an incandescent lamp has none
An LED has no terminals, but an incandescent lamp has two

stem: The two terminals of an incandescent lamp are fixed so that they do not touch each other. What would most likely happen if the two thick wires touched each other just below the filament?
options: The filament would glow more brightly than before
No current would flow in any part of the circuit
Current would skip the filament, so it stays dark
It would glow, but only if the cell were reversed
explanation: Correct option: (C). The filament glows only when current passes through it. If the thick wires touch, current finds a path through them that does not include the filament, so the filament does not glow. It would not glow more brightly, current still flows through the touching wires, and reversing the cell makes no difference to an incandescent lamp.

stem: When does a lamp connected to an electric cell glow?

When both lamp terminals touch one cell terminal
When the wire covering is left on at both ends
When the wires give a complete path for current

stem: In an electrical circuit, the direction of electric current is taken to be:
options: from the negative to the positive terminal of the cell
from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell
from the lamp outwards to both terminals of the cell
from the switch to the positive terminal of the cell
explanation: Correct option: (B). By convention, current in a circuit is taken to flow from the positive terminal of the cell, through the circuit, to its negative terminal. The reverse direction is not the convention, and current does not start from the lamp or the switch, which are only parts of its path.

stem: An LED connected to a battery is glowing. If the two wires at the LED are interchanged, what will happen?
options: It stops glowing, as current passes it one way only
It glows more brightly than it did before
It glows as before, as direction does not matter
It glows, but with a different colour than before
explanation: Correct option: (A). Current can pass through an LED in one direction only: from its longer (positive) wire to its shorter (negative) wire. Interchanging the wires reverses it, so no current flows and it stops glowing. It cannot glow brighter, the same or in another colour, because no current passes through it.

stem: Megha joins an incandescent lamp to a cell and it glows. She then swaps the two wires at the terminals of the cell. What will she observe?
options: The lamp stops glowing, as current flows one way only
The lamp glows only if she turns the cell around too
The lamp still glows, as either terminal can go to +
The lamp flickers, as current now flows both ways
explanation: Correct option: (C). With an incandescent lamp it does not matter which terminal connects to the positive or negative terminal of the cell; it glows as long as the circuit is complete. One-way current is true of an LED, not of an incandescent lamp, turning the cell is not needed, and the current does not flow both ways.

stem: Arun has an LED whose two wires were cut to the same length, so he cannot tell its terminals apart. He has a working two-cell battery. Which plan will identify the positive terminal of the LED?
options: Join it both ways; when it glows, the wire on battery + is positive
Join it to one cell; the wire that warms up first is the positive
Look inside it; the wire joined to the filament is the positive
Join both wires to battery +; the brighter end is the positive
explanation: Correct option: (A). An LED glows only when its positive terminal is joined to the positive terminal of the battery, so connecting it one way and then the other shows which wire is positive. Warming is not a test of terminals, an LED has no filament, and joining both wires to one battery terminal leaves no complete circuit, so it will not glow at all.

It completes or breaks the path of the circuit
It changes the direction in which current flows

options: closed
complete
open
reversed
explanation: Correct option: (C). In the OFF position there is a gap in the circuit, so no current flows and we say the circuit is open. A closed or complete circuit is the ON position, and 'reversed' does not describe a switch position.

stem: In a switch made from two drawing pins and a safety pin, the lamp glows only when the safety pin touches the second drawing pin. Why?
options: The metal pin closes the gap and completes the path
The metal pin adds extra energy to the electric cell
The metal pin changes the direction of the current
The metal pin stops current from leaving the lamp
explanation: Correct option: (A). When the safety pin touches both drawing pins, it closes the gap, the circuit becomes closed and current flows, so the lamp glows. The pin does not give energy to the cell or change the current's direction, and stopping current would make the lamp go off, not glow.

stem: Ali puts the switch between the negative terminal of the cell and the lamp, instead of between the positive terminal and the lamp. What happens when he turns the switch ON?
options: The lamp stays off, as a switch must be next to the + end
The lamp glows only while the switch is in the OFF position
The lamp glows dimly, as current now passes it backwards
The lamp glows, as a switch may be placed anywhere in it
explanation: Correct option: (D). A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit; when it is ON the path is complete and the lamp glows. It need not be next to the positive terminal, a lamp never glows with the switch OFF, and the position of the switch does not change the current or the brightness.

stem: A cell, two lamps and two switches S1 and S2 are all joined one after another in a single loop. Under which condition will both lamps glow?
options: Only S1 is ON, S2 is OFF
Only S2 is ON, S1 is OFF
Both S1 and S2 are ON
Both S1 and S2 are OFF
explanation: Correct option: (C). In a single loop, current has only one path, so any switch that is OFF leaves a gap and opens the whole circuit. Both lamps glow only when both switches are ON and the loop is complete. With either switch OFF, or both OFF, no current flows and neither lamp glows.

stem: Why do bodies such as the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) set standard symbols for electrical parts?

So each country can draw its own form of every part
So people everywhere can read circuit drawings easily
So only trained engineers are able to read the drawings

stem: Silver is among the best conductors of electricity, yet most electrical wires are made of copper. Why?

Silver does not let any current pass
Copper conducts better than all metals
Copper costs less and is found in plenty

stem: A student forgets to remove the plastic covering from the ends of the connecting wires while making a circuit. The lamp and the cell are working. Will the lamp glow?
options: No, as the plastic does not let current reach the metal
Yes, as the metal wire inside the cover still conducts
Yes, but dimly, as a little current leaks through it
Yes, but only after the cell is turned the other way
explanation: Correct option: (A). Plastic is an insulator. With the covering on the ends, the metal of the wires never touches the terminals, so the circuit is not complete and the lamp does not glow. The metal inside conducts only if it is in contact, insulation does not let a little current leak through, and turning the cell does not remove the insulation.

stem: An electrician's screwdriver has a metal tip and a thick plastic handle. Which is the best reason for this design?
options: The plastic handle is used only to give the tool colour
The plastic handle makes current flow faster in the tip
The plastic handle stops current reaching the user's hand
The metal tip blocks current so the handle stays cool
explanation: Correct option: (C). Our body is a conductor, so current passing through it can cause injury. Plastic is an insulator, so the handle keeps current away from the user's hand while the metal tip works on metal parts. The handle is not just decoration, an insulator does not speed up current, and metal is a conductor, so the tip does not block current.
